Quiz from Assessments (Mid-Term)

                                 ENG511_Psycholinguistics
                             Quiz from Assessments (Mid-Term)

1. Long-term memory is divided into semantic memory and ___________memory. (episodic)
2. We are not able to store more than seven words in our working memory. (False)
3. Our ____________ memory deals with personally experienced facts. (episodic)
4. The memories related to our childhood are the part of our _______________ memory.
   (semantic)
5. Connectionism is _________________ (Parallel processing)
6. Semantic memory holds general knowledge, whereas episodic memory stores our experience
   from our personal perspective. (incorrect)
7. In _____________________ information at the higher levels may influence processing at the
   lower levels. (top-down processing)
8. We receive auditory information, convert it into a neural signal and process the phonetic
   feature information. (Bottom-up)
9. Speech production is a product of nature and nurture. (Correct)
10.When we use stored information about language and the world to make sense of the speech, it
   is a _________________ process. (Top-down)
11.The phonetic segment is converted into a phoneme, and phonological rules are applied to the
   sound sequence. (Phonological level)
12.According to motor theory, infants can hear certain phonetic distinctions well before they are
   able to produce them. (True)
13.The perception of continuous speech, clearly indicates that word recognition is influenced by
   prosodic factors such as stress and intonational patterns. (True)
14.The visual stimulus is represented more abstractly as an identity separate from its physical
   manifestation is called ___________ of written language. (letter level)
15.At word level, the features and letters are recognized as a familiar word. (Correct)
16.Psycholinguists investigate the brain mechanism associated with language and the social rules
   involved in language use. (Incorrect)
17.Psycholinguists investigate the brain mechanism associated with language and the social rules
   involved in language use. (True)
18.The diversity of how we use language is daunting for ____________ who wish to study a
   language. (Psycholinguists)
19.Is this statement correct or incorrect? Language comprehension deals with the perception and
   understanding of speech and written language. (Incorrect)
20.Choose the correct option. The study of psycholinguistics is part of the field of
   _________science. (cognitive)
21.An integration of the fields of psychology and linguistics is called ________.
   (Psycholinguistics)
22.Halliday and Hasan (1976) define ____________ as referring to ‘‘the range of possibilities
   that exist for linking something with what has gone before’’. (cohesion)
23.Comprehension of connected discourse does not depend less on the meanings of the individual
   sentences than on their arrangement. (Incorrect)

Maha Malik’s Compilation

                                  ENG511_Psycholinguistics
                              Quiz from Assessments (Mid-Term)

24.Reference is a ____________relation whereby information needed for the interpretation of one
   item is found elsewhere in the text. (semantic)
25.The acceptability of discourse depends on the coherent relationship between its segments.
   (correct)
26.When subjects were in the TOT state, they retrieved but rejected similar-sounding word (True)
27.Tip-of -the-tongue (TOT) phenomenon occurs, when we are quite successful at retrieving a
   particular word and can remember something about how it sounds. (incorrect)
28.According to which of the following views, do the linguists consider phonology to be different
   from the rest of the language faculty, belonging to the Periphery rather than the Core? (Isolative
   view)
29.Phonology is a laboratory science, and linguists argues for the adoption of scientific
   methodology to test formal is a __________________ view. (Integrational)
30.The advantage of using syntactic categories is that we can formulate grammatical rules in terms
   of categories rather than lexical items. (Correct)
31.Agrammatic patients frequently omit __________________ from their sentences while
   preserving open-class words somewhat better. (closed-class words)
32.Morphemes are the smallest unit of meaning in a language. A word cannot consist of a single
   morpheme. (False)
33.Inflectional morphemes are involved when a__________ morpheme is added to a free
   morpheme to express grammatical contrasts in sentences. (bound)
34.Our ability to form various alternative forms of root words effectively means that there is a
   limit to the number of new words in a language. (Incorrect)
35.The jargon terminology may be taught directly depending on the grade and the cognitive level
   of the student. (True)

Psycholinguistics: The study of how humans acquire, process, and use
language, examining the psychological and neurobiological factors that
underlie language development, comprehension, and production
The Nature of Language: Psycholinguistics: Language is a complex,
dynamic system that involves cognitive processes, social interactions, and
cultural influences, which psycholinguistics seeks to understand.
The Scope of Psycholinguistics: Encompasses language development,
language processing, language disorders, language teaching, and language
acquisition, exploring the cognitive, social, and biological aspects of
language.
Language Processes and Linguistic Knowledge: Psycholinguistics
examines how we process language (e.g., perception, comprehension,
production) and how we acquire and represent linguistic knowledge (e.g.,
phonology, syntax, semantics).
The Historical Context: Early psycholinguistics emerged in the 1950s,
influenced by linguistics, psychology, and philosophy, with key figures like
Noam Chomsky, Eric Lenneberg, and George Miller.
Early Psycholinguistics: Focused on language acquisition, language
universals, and the innateness of language, with Chomsky's generative
grammar theory being a significant milestone.
The Information-Processing System: A cognitive framework that views
language processing as a series of stages, from input (perception) to output
(production), involving working memory and long-term memory.
Working Memory and Long-term Memory: Working memory temporarily
holds and manipulates language information, while long-term memory stores
linguistic knowledge and language representations.
Central Issues in Language Processing: Include language ambiguity,
language context, language development, language disorders, and language
universals.

Examples of Language Processing: Language comprehension (e.g.,
understanding sentences), language production (e.g., speaking), and language
acquisition (e.g., learning vocabulary).
Development of Processing System: Language processing abilities develop
in children through exposure to language, social interaction, and cognitive
maturation.
Developing Working and Long Term Memory: Children's working
memory and long-term memory capacities expand as they develop language
skills and cognitive abilities.
Language Comprehension: The process of interpreting language meaning,
involving semantic, syntactic, and pragmatic processing.
Perception of Language: The initial stage of language processing, involving
the recognition of speech sounds, words, and sentences.
The Structure of Speech: Speech consists of phonemes (smallest units of
sound), phonology (sound patterns), and prosody (rhythm and intonation).
Perception of Isolated Speech Segments: Listeners recognize individual
speech sounds and phonemes, which are the building blocks of language.
The Motor Theory of Speech Perception: Proposes that speech perception
is closely tied to speech production, suggesting that listeners use their own
motor experiences to recognize spoken language.
Perception of Continuous Speech: The process of recognizing spoken
language in real-time, involving the ability to segment and identify individual
sounds, words, and phrases.
Perception of Written Language: The process of recognizing and
interpreting written text, involving the ability to decode letters, words, and
sentences.
Phonological Knowledge: The mental representation of sound patterns in
language, including phonemes, syllables, and prosody.
Phonological Knowledge: Conceptual and Empirical Issues: Examines the
nature of phonological knowledge, its acquisition, and the empirical methods
used to study it.
Syntactic Knowledge: The mental representation of grammatical rules and
structures, including phrase structure, word order, and sentence formation.

Children's Acquisition of Syntactic Knowledge: The process by which
children learn and develop syntactic knowledge, including the role of input,
interaction, and cognitive development.
Morphological Knowledge: The mental representation of the internal
structure of words, including roots, prefixes, and suffixes.
Evaluating the Effectiveness of a Morphological Awareness Intervention:
Assessing the impact of instructional programs aimed at improving
morphological knowledge and reading skills.
Semantic Knowledge: The mental representation of word meanings,
concepts, and relationships between them.
The Concept of a Semantic Network: A theoretical framework representing
semantic knowledge as a network of interconnected nodes and associations.
Hierarchical Network Models: A type of semantic network model featuring
a hierarchical organization of concepts and categories.
Spreading Activation Models: A type of semantic network model where
activation spreads from one node to neighboring nodes, influencing semantic
processing.
Advantages and Disadvantages of Semantic Differential Scale: A
measurement tool used to assess semantic knowledge and connotative
meanings, with both benefits (e.g., quantifiable data) and limitations (e.g.,
oversimplification).
Semantic Barriers: Obstacles to effective communication arising from
differences in semantic knowledge, conceptual frameworks, or linguistic
expressions.
Difference Between Logogen and Cohort Model: Two theoretical models
of lexical access, with the logogen model positing a single, abstract
representation of words and the cohort model proposing multiple, context-
dependent representations.
Variables that Influence Lexicon Access: Factors affecting the retrieval of
words from memory, including frequency, context, and semantic priming.
Lexical Ambiguity: Words or phrases with multiple meanings, requiring
context to disambiguate.

Appraising Models of Lexical Access: Evaluating theories of how we
retrieve words from memory, including logogen, cohort, and connectionist
models.
Stages of Lexis in Speech Production: The process of word selection,
phonological encoding, and articulation in speech production.
Parsing: The process of analyzing sentence structure and meaning, involving
syntactic and semantic processing.

Lesson-01
                         INTRODUCTION TO
                        PSYCHOLINGUISTICS
Topic-001: Introduction to Psycholinguistics
What is psycholinguistics?
Psycholinguistics is the study of how individuals comprehend, produce, and acquire
language.
What fields contribute to cognitive science?
Cognitive science integrates psychology, linguistics, artificial intelligence,
neuroscience, and philosophy.
What are the main areas of interest in psycholinguistics?
Psycholinguistics focuses on language knowledge, cognitive processes in language
use, social rules in language, and brain mechanisms related to language.
When did contemporary interest in psycholinguistics begin?
Contemporary interest in psycholinguistics started in the 1950s, with important
precursors in the 20th century.
What is psycholinguistics, and how does it relate to cognitive science?

 COMPILED BY SIR ZAHID                                                         1

Psycholinguistics is the study of how individuals comprehend, produce, and acquire
language, and it is part of the field of cognitive science. Cognitive science draws
insights from psychology, linguistics, artificial intelligence, neuroscience, and
philosophy. Psycholinguistics focuses on language knowledge, cognitive processes
in language use, social rules in language use, and the brain mechanisms associated
with language. Interest in psycholinguistics began in the 1950s, building on earlier
work in the 20th century.
Topic-002: The Nature of Language: Psycholinguistics
Why is language important in human society?
Language is crucial in human society because it allows for the organization of a
civilized society and is the primary tool for communicating thoughts and feelings.
What are the three primary sets of processes in the psychology of language?
The three primary sets of processes in the psychology of language are language
comprehension, language production, and how people use language.
How does language evolve as children grow?
Language evolves from basic communication to serving various functions,
including the development of age-specific jargon.
Why is language important in human society, and what does the psychology of
language study?
Language is crucial because it enables the organization of a civilized society and
serves as a tool for communication. The psychology of language explores mental
processes involved in language use, including language comprehension (how we
understand speech and written language), language production (how we construct
utterances), and how people use language in various contexts.
Topic-003: The Scope of Psycholinguistics
What is cognitive science?
Cognitive science is an interdisciplinary field that combines insights from
psychology, linguistics, computer science, neuroscience, and philosophy to study
the mind and mental processes.
What makes psycholinguistics an interdisciplinary field?
Psycholinguistics integrates psychology and linguistics, drawing from diverse
intellectual traditions.
What is cognitive science, and why is psycholinguistics considered an
integration of psychology and linguistics?

 COMPILED BY SIR ZAHID                                                           2

Cognitive science is an interdisciplinary field that draws upon insights from
psychology, linguistics, computer science, neuroscientists, and philosophy to study
the mind and mental processes. Psycholinguistics primarily integrates psychology
and linguistics, although it has a rich heritage with contributions from various
intellectual traditions.
Topic-004: Language Processes and Linguistic Knowledge
What is the distinction between tacit and explicit knowledge?
Tacit knowledge refers to knowing how to do something without consciously
knowing how, while explicit knowledge involves knowing the processes or
mechanisms.
What are the four broad areas of language knowledge?
The four areas are semantics (meanings of sentences and words), syntax
(grammatical arrangement), phonology (sounds), and pragmatics (social rules).
What are the two main questions in psycholinguistics regarding language?
Psycholinguistics asks, "What knowledge of language is needed for us to use
language?" and "What cognitive processes are involved in the ordinary use of
language?"
What are the two main questions at the core of psycholinguistic work?
Psycholinguistic work focuses on two primary questions: 1) What knowledge of
language is necessary for using language? and 2) What cognitive processes are
involved in the ordinary use of language? These questions involve exploring both
tacit and explicit knowledge of language and the cognitive processes during
language use.
Topic-005: The Historical Context
What were the two periods of interdisciplinary activity in psycholinguistics?
There were two periods: one around the turn of the last century and another in the
mid-20th century, separated by decades of behaviorism.
How did the relationship between linguists and psychologists change during
these periods?
In the early 20th century, linguists sought insights from psychologists, and in the
mid-20th century, psychologists turned to linguists for insights into language.
How can the history of psycholinguistics be divided into two periods, and what
were the dominant views during these periods?

 COMPILED BY SIR ZAHID                                                          3

The history of psycholinguistics can be divided into two periods of interdisciplinary
activity. The first period, around the turn of the last century, was dominated by
cognitive views of language, particularly by Wilhelm Wundt. The second period, in
the mid-20th century, emerged in response to behaviorist views, with Noam
Chomsky challenging these views and emphasizing the role of innate linguistic
mechanisms.

psycholinguistics?

Lesson 06

                          LEXICAL ACCESS
Topic-032: Difference Between Logogen and Cohort Model
What is the key feature of Morton's Logogen Model?
The key feature is the interaction between sensory and contextual information.
How does the Logogen model account for facilitation effects in word
recognition?
It accounts for facilitation effects by allowing more contextual information to
reduce the need for sensory information to activate a Logogen.
What is the "critical recognition point" in Cohort Theory?
It is the point at which a word can be uniquely distinguished from other words in
the initial cohort based on sensory information.
Explain the key feature of Morton's Logogen Model, and how does it impact
lexical access?

 COMPILED BY SIR ZAHID                                                          1

Morton's Logogen Model introduces a crucial feature where both sensory and
contextual information interact. This interaction establishes a trade-off relationship
between them, where the more contextual information is provided to a Logogen
from top-down sources, the less sensory information is required to activate the
Logogen above threshold for activation. This feature allows the model to explain
the facilitation effects observed in word recognition, such as the impact of
syntactic and semantic constraints on the speed of lexical access, word frequency,
and word apprehension effects reported in the literature. In the presence of
constraining prior contexts, the time needed to activate a Logogen from the onset
of the relevant sensory information is reduced because less sensory information is
necessary to surpass the threshold value.
Topic-033: Variables That Influence Lexicon Access
Name one variable that affects lexicon access.
Word Frequency.
How does word frequency influence lexicon access?
More common words are accessed more readily than less frequent words.

Lexical ambiguity occurs when a single word has more than one meaning.

Define lexical ambiguity and provide an example of a sentence containing

Lexical ambiguity refers to a linguistic phenomenon where a single word can be
interpreted in multiple ways or has more than one meaning. An example of a
sentence containing lexical ambiguity is: "The man started to drill before the truck
arrived." In this sentence, the word "drill" can be interpreted as either the verb

2. Whorf Hypothesis (Sapir-Whorf Hypothesis)

The hypothesis posits that language determines or influences thought. There are two versions:

Major criticisms include:

      Overstating language’s control over thought.
      Lack of empirical support.
      Thought can occur without language (e.g., visual thinking).

This theory claims thought cannot exist without language. Inadequacies include:

Introduction to Psycholinguistics

Psycholinguistics is the study of how individuals comprehend, produce, and acquire language.
Psycholinguists are also interested in the social rules involved in language use and brain

in 1946 due to his student Nichols Hennry. Psycholinguistics as a separate branch of study
emerged in the late 1950s and 1960s as a result of Chomskyan revolution.

Topic-134: Operating Principles

One of the most productive approaches to the question has been Slobin’s work on operating principles. We may
think of operating principles as children’s preferred ways of taking in (or operating on) information. These
principles have proven useful in explaining certain patterns in early child grammar. For instance, children in
virtually all languages use fixed word order to create meanings, even though some languages have much freer word
order than others.

Topic-135: Sensorimotor Schemata

Piaget refers to the first 2 years as the sensorimotor period of development because the schemata the child uses to
organize experience are directly related to taking in sensory information and acting on it. Sensorimotor schemata
include banging, sucking, and throwing. The major development that culminates near the end of the sensorimotor
period is the acquisition of object permanence, the notion that objects continue to exist even when they cannot be
perceived. Once object permanence is acquired, the child is no longer at the mercy of immediate stimuli but can
respond on the basis of stimuli no longer present. We would certainly anticipate that developments of this magnitude
would be related to the child’s language development. More specifically, we can make two predictions about child
language.

Topic-136: Whole Object Bias and Taxonomic Bias

Whole object bias in developmental psychology: For example, if a child is shown and given the label "truck", the
child will assume truck refers to the whole object instead of the tires, doors, colors or other parts. If a researcher
points to an object while simultaneously saying a new name, children will assume that the new label refers to the
whole object. Ellen Markman pioneered work in this field. Her studies suggest that even in cases where color or
dynamic activities are made salient to children, they will still interpret the new word as a label for whole objects.
Furthermore, infants hold a primitive theory of the physical world that is guided by three constraints on the behavior
of physical bodies: objects must move as wholes, objects move independently of each other, and objects move on
connected paths. It is suggested that these three constraints help guide children’s interpretations of scenes, and, in
turn, explain how the whole object bias reflects the nonlinguistic status of objects.

In addition, children seem to use a taxonomic bias: they will assume that the object label is a taxonomic category
rather than a name for an individual dog. For example, they will assume that dog is a label for a group of animals,
not just Fido. Ordinarily, children focus on thematic relations between objects when categorizing. If given milk, a
spoon, or a car, children will group each item with a cow, soup, or a stop sign, respectively.

Topic-139: The Language Bioprogram Hypothesis

Maha Malik’s Compilation                                                                                      Page 1

                      ENG511 {Short Notes from Lesson(23-45)}
Pidgins and Creoles: To understand this idea more fully, we have to make a few distinctions. A pidgin is ‘an
auxiliary language that arises when speakers of several mutually unintelligible languages are in close contact’
(Bickerton, 1984, p. 173). Typically this occurs when workers from diverse countries are brought in as cheap labor
in an agricultural community. Immigrant workers come to speak a simpler form of the dominant language of the
area—just enough to get by. A creole occurs when the children of these immigrants acquire a pidgin as their native
language. Because access to native speakers of the dominant language is usually limited, these children receive the
impoverished pidgin version as their primary linguistic input. Bickerton (1983) observes that the conditions
necessary to produce creoles have existed numerous times between 1500 and 1900 when various European nations
developed labor-intensive agricultural economies on isolated, under populated tropical islands throughout the world.
Bickerton’s studies have focused on creoles in Hawaii. Although Hawaiian contact with Europeans goes back to the
18th century, it was not until 1876 that a revision of the U.S. tariff laws led to a large influx of indentured workers to
harvest Hawaiian sugar. Because Hawaiian creole developed between 1900 and 1920, it was possible for Bickerton
to study the development of the creole by studying the speech of people who are still living. In particular, he
examined the language of immigrants who moved to Hawaii and that of their children who were born in the first two
decades of the 20th century. The speech of pidgin speakers was rudimentary. In many cases, there was no
recognizable syntax, and the language resembled a linguistic free-for-all. Some speakers used one word order and
others another; the word orders were often related to the speaker’s own native language. Moreover, complex
sentences were absent in pidgin: pidgin sentences had no subordinate clauses, and even single-clause utterances
often lacked verbs. In addition, there was no consistent system of anaphora.

Topic-140: The Language Bioprogram

Unlike pidgins, the creoles resembled the structural rules of other languages. From these observations, Bickerton
concludes that children have an innate grammar that, in the absence of proper environmental input, serves as the
child’s language system. He calls this system the language bio program. Bickerton (1984) has responded to other
possible interpretations of his research. One is that the sophistication found in the children’s creoles was based on
their access to English, the language of the plantation owners. Bickerton points out, however, that contact between
immigrant families and owners was limited and that the Hawaiian creole differed in several respects from English.

respond on the basis of stimuli no longer present. We would certainly anticipate that developments of this magnitude
would be related to the child’s language development. More specifically, we can make two predictions about child
language.

Topic-136: Whole Object Bias and Taxonomic Bias

Whole object bias in developmental psychology: For example, if a child is shown and given the label "truck", the
child will assume truck refers to the whole object instead of the tires, doors, colors or other parts. If a researcher
points to an object while simultaneously saying a new name, children will assume that the new label refers to the
whole object. Ellen Markman pioneered work in this field. Her studies suggest that even in cases where color or
dynamic activities are made salient to children, they will still interpret the new word as a label for whole objects.
Furthermore, infants hold a primitive theory of the physical world that is guided by three constraints on the behavior
of physical bodies: objects must move as wholes, objects move independently of each other, and objects move on
connected paths. It is suggested that these three constraints help guide children’s interpretations of scenes, and, in
turn, explain how the whole object bias reflects the nonlinguistic status of objects.

In addition, children seem to use a taxonomic bias: they will assume that the object label is a taxonomic category
rather than a name for an individual dog. For example, they will assume that dog is a label for a group of animals,
not just Fido. Ordinarily, children focus on thematic relations between objects when categorizing. If given milk, a
spoon, or a car, children will group each item with a cow, soup, or a stop sign, respectively.

Topic-139: The Language Bioprogram Hypothesis

Maha Malik’s Compilation                                                                                      Page 1

                      ENG511 {Short Notes from Lesson(23-45)}
Pidgins and Creoles: To understand this idea more fully, we have to make a few distinctions. A pidgin is ‘an
auxiliary language that arises when speakers of several mutually unintelligible languages are in close contact’
(Bickerton, 1984, p. 173). Typically this occurs when workers from diverse countries are brought in as cheap labor
in an agricultural community. Immigrant workers come to speak a simpler form of the dominant language of the
area—just enough to get by. A creole occurs when the children of these immigrants acquire a pidgin as their native
language. Because access to native speakers of the dominant language is usually limited, these children receive the
impoverished pidgin version as their primary linguistic input. Bickerton (1983) observes that the conditions
necessary to produce creoles have existed numerous times between 1500 and 1900 when various European nations
developed labor-intensive agricultural economies on isolated, under populated tropical islands throughout the world.
Bickerton’s studies have focused on creoles in Hawaii. Although Hawaiian contact with Europeans goes back to the
18th century, it was not until 1876 that a revision of the U.S. tariff laws led to a large influx of indentured workers to
harvest Hawaiian sugar. Because Hawaiian creole developed between 1900 and 1920, it was possible for Bickerton
to study the development of the creole by studying the speech of people who are still living. In particular, he
examined the language of immigrants who moved to Hawaii and that of their children who were born in the first two
decades of the 20th century. The speech of pidgin speakers was rudimentary. In many cases, there was no
recognizable syntax, and the language resembled a linguistic free-for-all. Some speakers used one word order and
others another; the word orders were often related to the speaker’s own native language. Moreover, complex
sentences were absent in pidgin: pidgin sentences had no subordinate clauses, and even single-clause utterances
often lacked verbs. In addition, there was no consistent system of anaphora.

Topic-140: The Language Bioprogram

Unlike pidgins, the creoles resembled the structural rules of other languages. From these observations, Bickerton
concludes that children have an innate grammar that, in the absence of proper environmental input, serves as the
child’s language system. He calls this system the language bio program. Bickerton (1984) has responded to other
possible interpretations of his research. One is that the sophistication found in the children’s creoles was based on
their access to English, the language of the plantation owners. Bickerton points out, however, that contact between
immigrant families and owners was limited and that the Hawaiian creole differed in several respects from English.

Topic-134: Operating Principles

One of the most productive approaches to the question has been Slobin’s work on operating principles. We may
think of operating principles as children’s preferred ways of taking in (or operating on) information. These
principles have proven useful in explaining certain patterns in early child grammar. For instance, children in
virtually all languages use fixed word order to create meanings, even though some languages have much freer word
order than others.

Topic-135: Sensorimotor Schemata

organize experience are directly related to taking in sensory information and acting on it. Sensorimotor schemata
